heuristics.rule: If a sponsor asks you to pay any H-1B filing fees, stop the process immediately regardless of how legitimate they otherwise appear
heuristics.condition: When any employer or staffing firm requests payment for I-129 petition fees, ACWIA training fees, premium processing, or attorney fees...
heuristics.action: ...treat it as a definitive scam signal and exit the arrangement
heuristics.because: Charging workers for H-1B fees is explicitly illegal under INA § 212(n), so any company doing this is already in violation of federal law before you've even started

heuristics.rule: If a company offers H-1B sponsorship without being able to describe specific job duties, SOC code, wage level, and worksite, the petition is likely fraudulent
heuristics.condition: When a potential sponsor cannot articulate exactly what work you will do before filing...
heuristics.action: ...decline the offer, because the H-1B will be filed with incorrect or fabricated information
heuristics.because: Legitimate H-1B sponsorship requires a specific job with specific details; vagueness means the employer is either misrepresenting the role or filing fraudulently

heuristics.rule: If an H-1B sponsorship offer arrives within days of a first conversation with a firm you don't know, treat it as a red flag, not a win
heuristics.condition: When sponsorship is offered extremely fast before any real vetting of your role...
heuristics.action: ...slow down and conduct due diligence rather than accepting out of relief or urgency
heuristics.because: Legitimate sponsors have internal approval processes and established attorney relationships; speed signals the offer is not grounded in a real role

heuristics.rule: Never use the immigration attorney provided by the body shop to assess your compliance situation
heuristics.condition: When you are already in a problematic body shop arrangement and need legal advice...
heuristics.action: ...hire an independent immigration attorney, even if it costs money
heuristics.because: The employer's attorney represents the employer, not you; their advice will protect the company's interests, not yours

heuristics.rule: If you've been in H-1B status for 180+ days, you are not trapped — begin looking for a transfer immediately
heuristics.condition: When you are in a fraudulent or exploitative body shop but fear losing status if you leave...
heuristics.action: ...begin pursuing a new employer who can file an H-1B transfer rather than staying out of fear
heuristics.because: AC21 portability means your H-1B transfers to a new employer after 180 days without restarting the process

heuristics.rule: Search H-1Bdata.info or MyVisaJobs.com before accepting any offer from a small employer claiming to sponsor H-1B
heuristics.condition: When evaluating any small employer or staffing firm's sponsorship credibility...
heuristics.action: ...verify their petition history, occupation categories, and denial rates before proceeding
heuristics.because: A company with no H-1B history or high denial rates signals either inexperience or a pattern of fraudulent filings

decision_factors.factor: Whether employer pays all H-1B fees without exception
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Charging workers for fees is illegal and is the clearest single indicator of a fraudulent or non-compliant arrangement
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask directly and in writing whether you will be charged any fees related to the H-1B petition, filing, or legal process

decision_factors.factor: Specificity of the job role before petition filing
decision_factors.why_it_matters: H-1B petitions require specific job duties, SOC codes, and worksites; vagueness predicts a fraudulent petition that can harm your immigration record
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the employer to describe the exact position, SOC code they intend to file under, and the specific worksite location before agreeing to anything

decision_factors.factor: Verifiable H-1B petition history of the employer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A company that claims to sponsor regularly but has no public record of petitions is misrepresenting itself
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Cross-reference company name on H-1Bdata.info, MyVisaJobs.com, and USCIS public employer data

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Not paying during non-placement periods violates 20 CFR 655.731 and signals both legal non-compliance and financial instability of the sponsor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask explicitly: 'What is your policy on pay during periods between client placements?' and get it in writing

decision_factors.factor: Contract terms including non-compete and liquidated damages clauses
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Unusual financial penalties for resignation are used as leverage to keep workers in exploitative conditions even if technically unenforceable
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Have an independent attorney review any contract before signing; flag any clause requiring payment upon resignation

decision_factors.factor: Company's ability to name clients and connect you with current H-1B employees
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Legitimate staffing firms have real client relationships and satisfied employees; inability or refusal to provide either suggests the company may be operating on paper only
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask to speak with at least one current H-1B employee and ask for general client names; observe whether the firm hesitates or deflects

decision_factors.factor: Time remaining on OPT vs. urgency of accepting any sponsorship
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The comparison is not between a body shop and nothing — it is between a body shop and continued legitimate job searching under OPT; the calculus changes depending on how much OPT time remains
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate actual OPT expiration date including any STEM extension eligibility; determine how many months of runway you have for legitimate searching

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting body shop H-1B sponsorship to secure immigration status quickly
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Two years in a body shop often produces a weak or uncreditable employment history, a potentially non-compliant immigration record, and difficulty explaining the experience to future legitimate employers
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students near OPT expiration who feel no other option exists and accept out of panic rather than calculation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using the immigration attorney provided by the sponsoring body shop
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The attorney's professional obligation runs to the employer, not the worker; advice given will protect the company's interests, potentially at the worker's legal and immigration expense
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Workers already in problematic arrangements who assume that having an attorney means having representation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in a fraudulent body shop arrangement to avoid disrupting H-1B status
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the H-1B petition was filed incorrectly by the fraudulent firm, the worker may already be out of status without knowing it — staying longer does not fix this and may worsen it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Workers who conflate 'having a visa document' with 'being in valid immigration status'

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting resume coaching from a body shop to inflate experience for client placements
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Resume misrepresentation can affect the underlying H-1B petition's validity and potentially result in removal proceedings, creating permanent immigration consequences
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who feel pressure to comply with employer instructions and don't understand the immigration downstream effects

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in a body shop arrangement because leaving feels risky before the 180-day AC21 threshold
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Every additional day in a non-compliant arrangement increases potential immigration liability without providing the legal protection the worker believes they are accumulating
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Workers who know about AC21 portability but misunderstand what it protects them from

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting H-1B sponsorship from a body shop because it was the only offer and OPT expiration was imminent
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Visa deadline pressure creates tunnel vision — the comparison becomes 'this offer vs. deportation' rather than 'this offer vs. legitimate alternatives with remaining OPT time'
failure_patterns.consequence: Worker enters a fraudulent or non-compliant arrangement, may lose money, may have immigration record affected, and loses 12–24 months of legitimate career development
warning_signs: Feeling relief rather than scrutiny when the sponsorship offer arrives
Skipping due diligence steps because 'there's no time'

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to verify the employer's H-1B history before accepting an offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students are not taught that public petition data exists or how to use it; they assume that a formal offer letter signals legitimacy
failure_patterns.consequence: Worker discovers post-filing — or post-admission into the U.S. — that the employer has a history of denied or fraudulent petitions
warning_signs: Never having checked H-1Bdata.info or USCIS employer data
Accepting the employer's description of their sponsorship history at face value

failure_patterns.pattern: Complying with instructions to misrepresent experience on resumes for client placements
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Workers feel dependent on the sponsor for their immigration status and believe they cannot refuse employer instructions without risking their visa
failure_patterns.consequence: Resume fraud creates potential immigration fraud exposure that can affect all future visa applications and potentially result in removal proceedings
warning_signs: Employer provides a 'template' resume to adapt rather than asking for your actual experience
Employer coaches you on what to say in client interviews beyond legitimate preparation

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming the body shop's attorney is providing independent legal protection
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Workers conflate 'there is an attorney involved' with 'I have legal representation'; attorney involvement feels like procedural legitimacy
failure_patterns.consequence: Worker receives legal advice designed to protect the employer's interests, which may actively harm the worker's immigration position
warning_signs: Attorney was introduced or arranged by the employer rather than sought independently
Attorney answers questions in ways that seem to minimize worker concerns rather than address them

failure_patterns.pattern: Remaining in a body shop for two or more years because leaving felt risky
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Fear of disrupting H-1B status paralyzes action; workers overestimate the risk of leaving and underestimate the risk of staying
failure_patterns.consequence: Extended weak employment history, potential immigration non-compliance record, and missed window for legitimate OPT and sponsor search
warning_signs: Rationalizing staying because 'at least I have status'
Not knowing about AC21 portability rights after 180 days

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the employer asked you to pay any fees associated with the H-1B petition or immigration process?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Immediate indicator of illegal conduct; this is a binary disqualifier regardless of any other positive signals from the employer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Exit the arrangement immediately and consult an independent immigration attorney about your exposure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Get this confirmed in writing as part of the offer process and continue additional due diligence

diagnostic_questions.question: Can the employer describe your specific job duties, SOC code, wage level, and worksite before filing?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the H-1B petition will be filed with accurate information or fabricated to create the appearance of a real position
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Verify that what they describe matches the actual work you'll be doing and that the wage level is consistent with the prevailing wage for that role and location
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The employer cannot file a legitimate H-1B on your behalf; the offer is either premature or fraudulent

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the company's policy on pay during bench periods between client placements?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the employer understands and intends to comply with H-1B wage regulations requiring pay for the entire validity period
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Get the policy in writing and confirm it matches the regulatory requirement under 20 CFR 655.731
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The employer is either ignorant of or planning to violate H-1B wage requirements; either is a serious risk

diagnostic_questions.question: How much OPT time do you actually have remaining, including any STEM extension eligibility?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student is making a panic decision under artificial urgency or genuinely has no runway for continued legitimate job searching
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If significant OPT time remains, the true comparison is between this offer and 12+ more weeks of legitimate searching — reframe the decision accordingly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If OPT is genuinely expiring, explore cap-exempt employment options (universities, nonprofits) before accepting any body shop offer

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the company appear in H-1Bdata.info or USCIS employer data with a credible petition history?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company's claims about being an H-1B sponsor are consistent with public federal records
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Check the denial rate and the occupations they've sponsored for — a company that sponsors only one SOC code narrowly may be a body shop even if real
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The company has misrepresented its sponsorship history; treat all other representations with skepticism

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your current or prospective contract include non-compete clauses or liquidated damages for resignation?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the employer is using contract terms as leverage to trap workers in exploitative conditions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have an independent attorney review enforceability in your state before signing; do not sign under pressure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Continue due diligence on other dimensions; absence of predatory contract terms is necessary but not sufficient

industry_realities.common_belief: If a company gives you an offer letter and has an attorney filing your H-1B, the arrangement is legitimate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Fraudulent body shops routinely produce offer letters and use attorneys; the existence of paperwork and legal process involvement does not indicate compliance or legitimacy
industry_realities.implication: Workers must verify independently using public data, direct questions, and their own independent legal counsel rather than treating process as a proxy for legitimacy

industry_realities.common_belief: Not being paid during bench periods is unfair but legal — it's just part of the staffing model
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B regulations at 20 CFR 655.731 require employers to pay the offered wage for the entire validity period of the petition, including non-productive time
industry_realities.implication: Workers who are not paid during bench periods have a legal complaint they can file with the Department of Labor, and doing so is protected from retaliation

industry_realities.common_belief: Leaving a bad body shop arrangement will destroy your H-1B status and you'll have to start over
industry_realities.actual_reality: After 180 days of H-1B employment, AC21 portability allows workers to transfer to a new employer without restarting the H-1B cap process
industry_realities.implication: Workers are not trapped after 180 days; fear of status loss used to keep workers compliant is often unfounded and should be verified with an independent attorney

industry_realities.common_belief: The choice facing an international student near OPT expiration is between a body shop offer and losing status
industry_realities.actual_reality: The actual alternatives include continued OPT job searching, STEM OPT extension, and cap-exempt employment at universities and nonprofits which are not subject to the H-1B lottery
industry_realities.implication: Students should calculate their full runway of legitimate options before accepting any sponsorship offer under urgency pressure

industry_realities.common_belief: Resume coaching from your employer to help you get placed at clients is normal interview preparation
industry_realities.actual_reality: When body shops coach workers to misrepresent experience for client placements, this constitutes resume fraud that can affect the underlying H-1B petition and create permanent immigration consequences
industry_realities.implication: Workers should refuse any instruction to misrepresent qualifications regardless of employer pressure, and understand that compliance does not protect them from the consequences

industry_realities.common_belief: Financial penalties for leaving a job are standard and must be honored
industry_realities.actual_reality: Liquidated damages clauses and unusually large financial penalties for resignation in body shop contracts are often legally unenforceable but are designed to psychologically trap workers
industry_realities.implication: Workers should have an independent attorney assess enforceability before assuming they are bound, and should not let such clauses prevent them from leaving genuinely exploitative arrangements

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats receipt of an offer letter as validation of legitimacy; focuses on whether sponsorship is offered rather than how it is structured
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats offer letter as the beginning of due diligence; cross-references public petition data, asks specific questions about job duties and wage compliance, and seeks independent legal review before proceeding
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Fraudulent body shops are specifically designed to exploit the junior pattern; the offer letter is the bait, not the signal of safety

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Frames the choice as 'this body shop offer vs. losing my visa status' — a binary driven by fear
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Frames the choice as 'this offer vs. all legitimate alternatives including OPT runway, STEM extension, and cap-exempt employers' — a multi-option calculation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The binary framing produces panic-driven decisions that benefit fraudulent sponsors; the multi-option framing reveals that the body shop is rarely the only path

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes immigration status is entirely controlled by the employer and that any non-compliance by the employer reflects on or harms the worker
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Understands specific worker protections including wage violation complaint rights, retaliation protection, and AC21 portability; knows these rights exist and how to exercise them
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Ignorance of worker protections is what makes exploitation possible; knowing your rights changes the power dynamic

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Complies with employer instructions including resume coaching and misrepresentation because the employer controls the visa and refusing feels dangerous
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Distinguishes between legitimate employer direction and instructions that create legal exposure; understands that following illegal instructions does not protect you from their consequences
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Workers who comply with resume fraud instructions absorb the immigration risk without receiving any protection from the employer who directed them

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Using the attorney in the process
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes the attorney involved in the H-1B process represents their interests because they are 'the worker the attorney is helping'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Understands that the employer's attorney represents the employer; seeks independent legal counsel for any assessment of their personal compliance situation or exposure
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Relying on the employer's attorney for personal legal advice is one of the primary mechanisms by which workers in bad arrangements fail to understand or protect their position
